Lessons.Title: Divide Unit Fractions by Whole Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Purpose IM K-5 2021 Grade5 U03:L11: divide a UNIT fraction by a positive whole-number recipient count. The original reference stays the FULL pan; do not turn the fraction dividend into its reciprocal.
Warm-up — Number Talk Double the Divisor: the source sequence is 72÷4=18,36÷4=9,4÷4=1,1÷4=1/4. Pupils explain why a smaller starting quantity shared among four gives a smaller result.

Activity 1 — More Macaroni and Cheese: Jada AND HER TWO SISTERS (three people) equally share ONE HALF of an original pan. Draw full pan, highlight remaining half, subdivide the half into three equal pieces: EACH receives 1/6 OF THE ENTIRE PAN. Write (1/2)÷3=1/6; source MLR7 Compare and Connect gallery walk reviews diagrams and explanations.

Activity 2 — More People Share: FOUR people share the SAME half-pan so each gets 1/8 of the original whole; FIVE people share the half so each receives 1/10. Explain why increasing group count decreases the per-person portion; compare with three-person 1/6. The teacher evaluates equal partition dimensions and source drawing quality.

Assessment and source boundaries: independent Edulytiks-authored alternative Cool-down asks SIX people to share half a pan and explain 1/12 against the original full pan. Exact numeric subskills are only supplements: macaroni drawings, comparison discussion and MLR7 oral explanations remain TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED. Publisher-gated Cool-down, figure binaries and separate Student PDF not independently inspected.
Earlier mathematically valid 1/2 of a tray shared by four and 1/2 meter of ribbon shared by three are OPTIONAL EXTENSIONS, not original 2021 source activities.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit fraction divided by people
KeyConcepts.Definition: A selected part of a unit whole is distributed equally among several groups.
KeyConcepts.Example: Half a tray split among four people gives 1/8 tray each.

KeyConcepts.Title: Original whole matters
KeyConcepts.Definition: The final share is measured relative to the original entire tray or ribbon, not just the leftover portion.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Extend equal subdivisions to the original whole when naming the unit fraction.
KeyConcepts.Example: One quarter of a half is 1/8 of the original.

KeyConcepts.Title: Different roles in fraction division
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing a fraction by a whole is not dividing a whole by that same fraction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Activity 1: Jada and two sisters
WorkedExamples.Question: Three people divide half a pan of macaroni and cheese evenly. How much of the ORIGINAL FULL PAN does each receive?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original source context, equal-area full-pan model, and teacher-reviewed drawing.
Steps: Draw the whole pan and select one half.
Partition that half into three equal parts.
Extend the cut to the full pan and count six equal original-pan pieces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Activity 2: four share
WorkedExamples.Question: Four people share the same half-pan. How much per person?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original source context, equal-area full-pan model, and teacher-reviewed drawing.
Steps: Identify original whole pan and remaining 1/2.
Partition remaining half equally into four pieces.
Each person takes one of eight original-pan pieces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Activity 2: five share
WorkedExamples.Question: Five people share the same half-pan. How much per person?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original source context, equal-area full-pan model, and teacher-reviewed drawing.
Steps: Retain the half-pan as starting quantity.
Split that half into five equal pieces.
Each piece represents one tenth of the full original pan.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional extension — Divide a half tray
WorkedExamples.Question: Four people split half a tray of food equally. What portion of the full tray does each receive?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Shade one half of the original tray.
Divide the shaded half into four equal-area pieces.
Extend the four splits to obtain eight equal parts of the original whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional extension — Divide half a meter
WorkedExamples.Question: Three people share 1/2 meter of ribbon equally.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Keep one meter as the original whole.
Divide the selected 1/2 meter into three equal parts.
Compare each share with all six equal parts of the full meter.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional extension — Check division direction
WorkedExamples.Question: Are 1/2÷3 and 3÷1/2 equal?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Interpret the first as distributing half of one whole to three recipients.
Interpret the second as counting how many halves fit inside three wholes.
Calculate 1/6 versus 6 and explain why their units differ.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reverse a fractional dividend and integer divisor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The size and number of groups swap roles, changing the situation and quotient.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write the quantity being shared first and number of recipients second.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Report one quarter of the remaining half as a quarter of the full tray
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The selected half is not the original unit whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count resulting equal pieces across the whole tray before naming the final share.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Replace original macaroni-and-cheese three/four/five-person tasks with fabricated ribbon or bread story
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original 2021 source requires interpreting leftover half-pan and full-whole reference.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teach source macaroni stories first and preserve unrelated valid models as supplemental only.

SummaryPoints: Original macaroni and cheese: Jada and two sisters split 1/2 pan →1/6 each.
Four people split 1/2 pan →1/8, five people →1/10; original full pan is the unit.
The diagram and the partner explanation are teacher-reviewed, numeric choice alone insufficient.
Independent Cool-down: six people share 1/2 original pan → 1/12 each.

Lessons.Title: Represent Division of Unit Fractions by Whole Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Purpose IM K5 2021 Grade5 U03:L12: interpret and critique diagrams for a UNIT fraction shared by a positive whole number. A quotient is always stated relative to the original complete unit, not the selected third alone.

Warm-up Estimation Exploration: estimate a shaded region, compare the source tape and source area models for a quarter of a whole with a smaller selected region; allow justified too-low/about-right/too-high estimates. Approximate source publisher pictures cannot be assumed to give a uniquely exact area.

Activity 1 Diagrams Equations Situations: source Priya and Mai diagrams both show (1/3)÷4=1/12 OF THE SAME WHOLE, even though partitions have different orientations. Han draws (1/3)÷3=1/9. Students compare what the two diagrams preserve and identify the full original whole.

Activity 2 Priya's Work: source claims '(1/3)÷2=1/2' because half of the third is shaded; this is INCORRECT when reporting part of the whole. The true fraction is (1/3)÷2=1/6 of ORIGINAL WHOLE. Apply MLR3 Clarify, Critique, Correct; students write questions and a revised explanation rather than simply picking an answer.

Activity 3 Look for Patterns: original source expressions (1/4)÷2=1/8, (1/4)÷3=1/12, (1/4)÷4=1/16. Generalize (1/4)÷n = 1/(4n) for positive whole-number n; use teacher-reviewed equal partition models and verbal why.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two diagrams, one amount
KeyConcepts.Definition: A selected unit fraction can be subdivided locally or the entire whole can be repartitioned.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Both methods must create the same-sized tiny share relative to the original whole.
KeyConcepts.Example: 1/3÷4 is one of twelve equal whole-length parts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Tape diagram as a whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fixed full-length strip records the original unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Mark original unit endpoints, then label each equal subdivided group.
KeyConcepts.Example: The whole has 12 equal intervals after dividing one third into four parts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Check by repeated shares
KeyConcepts.Definition: The quotient multiplied by the number of equal recipients recovers the fractional dividend.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source diagram comparison Priya and Mai
WorkedExamples.Question: Use two orientations of the original whole to explain (1/3)÷4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide a selected third into four equal subparts, extending the whole-unit count.
Steps: Name one full original unit and its three equal thirds.
Divide one chosen third into four equal smaller pieces.
Show 12 equal parts in the ORIGINAL whole; one is selected.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source Priya flawed explanation
WorkedExamples.Question: Priya says (1/3)÷2 is 1/2. Critique and correct.
WorkedExamples.Method: Distinguish half of a selected third from a half of the original whole.
Steps: Keep the original whole as one unit.
Halve one of three equal thirds.
One of six original-whole equal cells is shaded.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 1/6 of the original whole; Priya's 1/2 is incorrect.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source quarter pattern
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate (1/4)÷2, (1/4)÷3 and (1/4)÷4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Hold a quarter of the whole and divide it into 2/3/4 equal shares.
Steps: Divide one original whole into fourths.
Subdivide the selected quarter by 2,3,4 respectively.
Count all equal full-whole pieces to obtain denominators 8,12,16.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Two valid tape diagrams
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain 1/3÷4 in two different ways.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: In diagram A mark the first third, then split it into four equal parts.
In diagram B mark twelve equal parts across the whole and select one.
Explain the selected small piece has the same length in both diagrams.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Divide one third by three
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 1/3÷3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Mark a third of an original one-unit tape.
Divide that third into three equal pieces.
Extend the marks and compare the small piece to nine equal whole-unit parts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Find a missing partner share
WorkedExamples.Question: One fourth of a sheet is split among two pupils. How much of the whole per pupil?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Mark one quarter of a complete sheet.
Halve that quarter into two equal regions.
Count eight equal resulting areas of the original sheet.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume two diagrams are incompatible if only one shows full-length subdivisions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Both can describe equivalent equal-area pieces when the unseen division is extended to the whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare actual ratios and extend all subdivisions to the original unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Compare a one-third strip to a one-third share rather than a whole-unit share
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The final denominator must express the original whole when the question says 'of the whole'.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Relabel the entire tape and count all tiny equal intervals.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mistake a fraction OF the selected third for a fraction OF the original whole
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Priya's source calculation 1/3÷2=1/2 uses the wrong reference whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Extend the partitions across the full unit: one of six equal full-whole pieces.

SummaryPoints: Original 1/3÷4=1/12 and 1/3÷3=1/9; teacher compares diagram orientations.
Priya's wrong 1/3÷2=1/2 must be corrected to 1/6 of original whole.
Quarter pattern 1/4÷2,3,4 yields 1/8,1/12,1/16.
Learner diagrams, critique and MLR3 peer discussion remain teacher reviewed.
Independent Edulytiks Cool-down asks (1/5)÷3=1/15 with original whole.

Visuals.Description: Edulytiks original numeric/tape model, not publisher artwork; exact full-whole reference; diagrams require teacher review.

Cells: half a third = one sixth whole

Lessons.Title: Divide Whole Numbers by Unit Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Purpose of IM 2021 U03:L13: count how many 1/b-foot-sized equal groups fit into an ORIGINAL WHOLE-NUMBER FEET LENGTH; do not confuse total length or units with the number of pieces. The source explicitly uses paper strips and quilt visual context.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder: Quilts — discuss the source Gee's Bend quiltmakers and rectangular fabric arrangements respectfully. Original photograph is credited CC BY 2.0 and is not copied without separate image rights verification. Different colored strips are measured in feet.

Activity 1 Paper Strips: the source gives THREE original strips, each exactly TWO FEET long. Red cut into 1/2-foot pieces produces 4; green 1/3-foot produces 6; yellow 1/4-foot produces 8. Explain why all originals have same 2-foot whole and why smaller fractional group size produces more pieces.

Activity 2 More Paper Strips: Kiran cuts a TWO-FOOT yellow strip into 1/6-foot pieces so 2÷(1/6)=12 pieces. Explain a distinct THREE-FOOT strip cut into 1/6-foot segments: 3÷(1/6)=18. Students draw, interpret actual equal intervals and describe the context of the quotient.
Students explain why 2÷(1/b)=2b, but dividing a unit fraction by 2 is a different operation. A prior correct 3-meter numerical example remains only an optional extension, not the source Activity 1.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole divided by a unit fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Counting how many 1/b-sized pieces fit into n whole units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Size of the group versus number of groups
KeyConcepts.Definition: Smaller piece sizes permit more pieces from the same positive total.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three meters contain fifteen fifth-meter pieces but six half-meter pieces.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit length context
KeyConcepts.Definition: The divisor describes the length of each piece, not the number of recipients.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check that piece count × piece length recovers the original total.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original three two-foot source strips
WorkedExamples.Question: How many pieces from 2 feet of red, green and yellow paper cut respectively into 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4 foot?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count unit-fraction-sized groups in a fixed original 2-foot strip.
Steps: Red: two whole feet with two half-feet per foot → four.
Green: three third-feet per foot → six.
Yellow: four quarter-feet per foot → eight.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source Kiran sixth-foot cuts
WorkedExamples.Question: Kiran cuts 2 feet of yellow strip into 1/6-foot pieces. How many?
WorkedExamples.Method: Group count from equivalent sixth-foot segments.
Steps: One foot has six pieces of length 1/6 foot.
Two feet contain 2×6 such pieces.
Explain what quotient means in the strip context.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source three-foot strip sixths
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain 3÷1/6=18 in feet-strip language.
WorkedExamples.Method: Three original one-foot units each contribute six sixth-foot pieces.
Steps: Start with 3 whole feet.
Split each full foot into six identical sixth-foot segments.
Count all 18 groups.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Half-meter pieces
WorkedExamples.Question: A 3-meter strip is cut into 1/2-meter pieces. How many?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Each meter contains two half-meter pieces.
Three meters contain three groups of two.
Count all six equal cuts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Third-meter pieces
WorkedExamples.Question: The same 3-meter strip is cut into 1/3-meter pieces.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Each meter contains three third-meter pieces.
Count three meters of three pieces.
Multiply 3×3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional existing extension — Quarter-meter pieces
WorkedExamples.Question: A 3-meter strip is cut into 1/4-meter pieces.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Each meter contains four quarter-meter pieces.
Repeat for three one-meter lengths.
Count 3×4 groups.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The operation asks the NUMBER of quarter-meter groups fitting in three meters.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count four quarters in each meter, then multiply by the number of meters.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use unequal cuts while claiming equal unit-fraction pieces
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The divisor describes one consistent fraction of a meter.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark equal 1/4-meter intervals and count all complete pieces.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use a three-meter strip as the original source's three paper strips
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: All three source Activity 1 paper strips are two FEET, so half/third/quarter counts are 4/6/8 not 6/9/12.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restore the source's two-foot red green yellow strips; use 3-foot only in the separate Activity 2 example and meter models only as extensions.

SummaryPoints: Original red, green, yellow strips each 2 feet: halves give 4, thirds 6, quarters 8.
Kiran's 2-foot yellow strip divided into sixths gives 12; separate 3-foot example gives 18.
Group count 2÷(1/b)=2b for positive whole b; do not use 3-meter substitute.
Teacher reviews actual physical strips, quilt context and drawings.
Independent Edulytiks paper strip Cool-down checks 4÷1/8=32 pieces.

Visuals.Description: Edulytiks original accessible source-number table; paper-strip drawings and source quilt photograph require separate teacher verification.

Lessons.Title: Represent Division of Whole Numbers by Unit Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: express, compare and generalize patterns in dividing whole numbers by a unit fraction, using number tables and optional tape diagrams. The 2021 source asks students to explore separate sets where the whole dividend or unit-fraction divisor changes and to explain the different patterns.
Warm-up: reason mentally how 6÷1, 6÷1/2, 6÷1/3 and 6÷1/6 change. Relate growing quotients to a fixed six-unit length divided into successively shorter pieces.

Activity 1 — hold divisor fixed: compute 2÷1/3=6, 3÷1/3=9, 4÷1/3=12, 5÷1/3=15. Use a labelled strip or verbal model to explain adding three pieces for each added whole unit. Describe the pattern without assuming that integer quotients alone prove the geometry.

Activity 2 — hold dividend fixed: compute 3÷1/2=6, 3÷1/3=9, 3÷1/4=12, 3÷1/5=15. Each answer is the number of fractional pieces in the same three units; denominators increasing by one add three groups. Compare the two patterns as a class, then test an original larger case 7÷1/6=42.

Assessment boundary: completing tables may be independently verified, but the source's gallery walk of explanations, diagram use and clear contrast between holding dividend or divisor fixed require teacher review. No original diagram cards and protected solutions are copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed unit-fraction divisor
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adding one whole unit adds b more 1/b-sized pieces.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed whole-number dividend
KeyConcepts.Definition: As the unit-fraction divisor becomes smaller, the piece count grows.

KeyConcepts.Title: Verify a division pattern
KeyConcepts.Definition: Pattern claims must agree with the meaning of division and exact multiplication.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fixed third-meter pieces
WorkedExamples.Question: Complete 2÷1/3,3÷1/3,4÷1/3,5÷1/3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Each whole has three one-third pieces.
Multiply each integer dividend by three.
Describe the +3 growth each time the dividend grows by one.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fixed three-unit length
WorkedExamples.Question: Complete 3÷1/2,3÷1/3,3÷1/4,3÷1/5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Keep the dividend three units.
Count how many b-ths fit into each whole.
Multiply three by each denominator b.

WorkedExamples.Title: Predict a sixth-sized piece count
WorkedExamples.Question: How many 1/6-sized pieces fit into seven whole units?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Each unit contains six such pieces.
Repeat seven times.
Multiply 7×6.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume both pattern tables change the same physical quantity
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One table changes the amount shared, the other changes the size of pieces.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label exactly which factor is the dividend and which is the unit-fraction divisor.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Interpret larger denominators as larger physical piece lengths
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: With a fixed unit whole, one fifth is shorter than one third.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare equal-unit pieces on a tape before predicting number of groups.

SummaryPoints: Two changing-quotient patterns can share results while describing different changes in a grouping situation.
For positive integers n,b, n÷(1/b)=nb.
Teacher reviews comparison posters and verbal pattern explanations.

Lessons.Title: Fraction Division Situations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: MATCH authentic story situations to equations for the two distinct types of fraction division taught in prior lessons. The source provides more expressions than stories and requires students to defend both correct and deliberately unmatched cards, then create their own division contexts.

Warm-up: compare 6÷(1/3)=18 with (1/3)÷6=1/18. Both contain the same two numbers, but their dividend/divisor order produces different quantities. Explain that one counts how many small groups fit in six, while the other shares a third among six recipients.

Activity 1 — original card sort: Story A says three meters of cloth are cut into 1/4-meter pieces; matching expression is 3÷(1/4)=12 pieces. Story B says 1/4 of a sheet is shared among three students; expression (1/4)÷3=1/12 sheet each. Include unmatched 3÷4 on the card set and explain why it is not a truthful model of either described situation.

Activity 2 — compose a new narrative for 2÷(1/5)=10 and contrast with (1/5)÷2=1/10. Students write the actual unit and question, make a tape or paper diagram, and exchange stories with a partner to test whether the division equation matches the story rather than only the numbers.

Assessment: source's card sorting, authoring, discussion and peer justification are open responses requiring human review. Numeric answer checking is possible for matched exact expressions, but must not certify the original task when the wrong card is chosen. Gated response cards and source artwork are not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Expression meaning is contextual
KeyConcepts.Definition: A dividend and a divisor can be a quantity and a group size, with distinct mathematical roles.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 3÷1/4 counts quarter-sized pieces in 3; 1/4÷3 splits a quarter into three shares.

KeyConcepts.Title: Check a story card
KeyConcepts.Definition: A correct match must represent the total quantity, number or size of groups, and unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Annotate the dividend/divisor and compute, then test against the story.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 meters cut into quarter-meter pieces gives 12 lengths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unmatched expressions are meaningful
KeyConcepts.Definition: A candidate expression may be numerically valid but not correspond to any supplied story.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Reject a card if its grouping or units don't match the story even when it has a computable value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Cloth strip story
WorkedExamples.Question: Three meters are cut into 1/4-meter pieces. Which division expression models how many pieces?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Identify three meters as total length.
Identify 1/4 meter as the size of EACH piece.
Divide 3 by 1/4 and count twelve quarter-meter pieces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Share a quarter sheet
WorkedExamples.Question: One fourth of a paper sheet is shared equally among three people. Which expression is correct?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: The amount shared is 1/4 of the full sheet.
There are three equal recipients.
Compute 1/4÷3=1/12 of a sheet each.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a wrong card
WorkedExamples.Question: Does 3÷4 represent three meters cut into quarter-meter pieces?
WorkedExamples.Method: Interpret equal-sized groups and the fixed whole with an original diagram before checking exact division.
Steps: Interpret 3÷4 as three divided into four equal groups.
Recognize the cloth story requires count of 1/4-meter groups, not four groups.
Replace the divisor 4 with 1/4 meter.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks the contextual explanation and units, not only the numeric result.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Match solely because the equation contains the story's two digits
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A whole number 4 and the unit fraction 1/4 describe very different divisor sizes.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Name the unit and 'size of group' in each story before selecting an expression.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat a valid numeric result as proof the card matches a story
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The numbers may be calculated correctly but answer a different question.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explain how every term of the expression corresponds to a specific story quantity.

SummaryPoints: Unit fraction ÷ whole and whole ÷ unit fraction describe different operations and situations.
Matching stories and expressions requires correct quantity roles, not shared printed numbers.
Writing and validating one's own stories is teacher-reviewed.
